newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. Gov signs new crime bills to protect police.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. Gov signs new crime bills to protect police.

text.p: New York Gov. George Pataki, saying fighting crime was his Administration's first priority, on Thursday signed three crime bills, including one that aims to give police, firemen and other workers more protection.

Pataki vowed that he would press for additional reforms, and told reporters at a news conference that "The fight against violent crime has been the most important priority of this Administration since the day I took office."
He noted his Administration already had reintroduced the death penalty and stiffened sentences for violent criminals, among other measures.

While applauding the new legislation, Frank Phillips, the head of the New York State Association of District Attorneys, said the state was not retreating from its history of safeguarding the rights of defendants.
"New York State has always been a leader in protecting the rights of criminal defendants and we all expect it will continue to do so," said Phillips, who is the District Attorney for Orange County.

The legislation, which overturns court decisions, goes into effect on November 1. One provision raises the penalty for intentionally thwarting police and peace officers, firemen and emergency medical workers from carrying out their duties and causing them serious physical injuries.

Last year, more than 10,000 police officers were injured in the line of duty, while three were killed and 14 were shot, said Frank Matarazzo, the president of the New York City Policemen's Benevolent Association. "This type of legislation means a whole lot," he said, adding he represented 28,000 police officers.
The new maximum sentence for these offenses will be 15 years; the current law sets a seven-year maximum jail sentence and also provides for probation.
Another measure ensures that when a defendant fails to appear in court, the prosecution no longer will be held accountable for the delays that result.

Pataki said New York State was unique because it has allowed defendants to get charges against them dismissed as the prosecution had not fulfilled the "speedy trial" standard. The state has counted the time the defendants spent as fugitives in applying this standard.

The last measure allows judges to excuse a juror who fails to appear for a reasonable amount of time, such as two hours, and substitute an alternate juror without being concerned their ruling will be reversed.
